title: Cross (X) Star Pattern
description: Brute force to optimized: dual-diagonal per-cell checks versus placing stars directly at the two known diagonal columns, then batching the whole pattern into one output call.

blocks.text: Given a positive integer n, print an n by n grid where a star appears on the main diagonal, where the row index equals the column index, and on the anti diagonal, where the row index plus the column index equals n minus 1, with a space everywhere else.

blocks.title: Analogy: Two Ribbons Crossing a Square Tile
blocks.text: Picture a square tile with two straight ribbons laid across it, one running from the top left corner to the bottom right corner, and the other from the top right corner to the bottom left corner. Together they cross exactly once, right in the middle, forming an X shape, while the rest of the tile is left bare.

blocks.caption: The main diagonal and the anti diagonal cross to form an X shape

blocks.text: With only 2 rows, both diagonal positions land on every cell, so the whole grid fills with stars.
A single cell, which sits on both diagonals at once, so it is simply a single star.

Every shape solved so far in this division has been built from one or two contiguous runs, a block of spaces followed by a block of stars. This shape looks similar at first glance, but it is worth checking whether that same contiguous-run idea still applies.

blocks.title: How Should We Think?
blocks.text:
Observation 1: Testing a small example, n equal to 5, shows the stars in a middle row like row 1, at columns 1 and 3, are not next to each other, there is a gap of plain space in between them, so this row is not one contiguous star run like the earlier shapes.

Observation 2: What is fixed instead is the exact count of star positions per row, always exactly two, at column i, the main diagonal, and column n minus 1 minus i, the anti diagonal, except when they coincide in the middle row.

Observation 3: Since exactly two column indices are already known for every row, the right technique is not to build a contiguous run at all, it is to start from an entirely blank row and place a star directly at each of those two known positions.

Observation 4: This is a genuinely different construction technique from the rest of this division, direct index placement into an otherwise blank row, instead of concatenating contiguous space and star runs.
Recognizing that a shape's stars are isolated points rather than a contiguous block is the signal to switch from "build runs and concatenate" to "start blank and place stars at known indices".
Use two nested loops covering every row and column, and for each individual cell, check whether its row and column indices satisfy either diagonal condition.

items: Loop over each row i and each column j inside it.
For every cell, check if i equals j, the main diagonal, or if i plus j equals n minus 1, the anti diagonal.
If either is true, print a star.
Otherwise print a space.

blocks.caption: Brute force flow: check both diagonal conditions for every single cell

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: Both diagonal conditions, i equals j and i plus j equals n minus 1, are checked together in a single expression, for every one of the n squared cells, even though at most two columns per row will ever satisfy either one.
The row loop and column loop are fully independent, so no information about which two columns actually matter for this row is carried forward, every column gets tested from scratch.
A single character, star or space, is printed per innermost iteration, keeping the per cell cost of this version fully visible.

blocks.text: This is correct, since every cell is individually tested against both diagonal conditions before deciding what to print.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n squared), since every one of the n squared cells requires its own two part condition check.
Space: O(1) extra space, no string is ever built.

Limitation: checking both diagonal conditions for every single cell is wasteful, since only two columns in each row can ever hold a star, column i and column n minus 1 minus i, every other position in that row is guaranteed to be blank. Testing all n columns individually adds nothing once those two positions are already known.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text:
Why checking every column works but is wasteful: for a given row, only 2 of its n columns will ever be a star, yet all n get individually tested against both diagonal conditions.

What is genuinely new here compared to earlier shapes in this division: those shapes always built one or two contiguous runs of the same character, here the two star positions are isolated points with plain space between them, so there is no contiguous star run to build at all.

What actually changes: instead of concatenating runs, start each row as entirely blank, then place a star directly at exactly the two already-known column indices.

Can a direct-construction technique still apply here: yes, just a different one, placing a value at a known index is just as direct an operation as building a run of known length.

The core idea: allocate a blank row of n spaces, then place a star at column i and at column n minus 1 minus i, the two positions already known before the row is built.

For each row i, start with a blank row of n spaces, then place a star directly at column i and column n minus 1 minus i, the only two positions that were ever going to hold one. This replaces n conditional checks per row with two direct placements.
For each row i, start with a blank row of n spaces, then place a star directly at the two known diagonal columns, and print the row once.

blocks.caption: Optimized flow: start blank, place a star at exactly the two known columns

codes.python:
def cross_pattern(n):
    for i in range(n):                          # only the two diagonal columns matter per row
        row = [" "] * n                            # start with a blank row of n spaces
        row[i] = "*"                                # the main diagonal position
        row[n - 1 - i] = "*"                        # the anti diagonal position
        print("".join(row))                       # one print call per row instead of per character


if __name__ == "__main__":
    cross_pattern(5)

blocks.text: This works because the two positions that must hold a star in row i, column i and column n minus 1 minus i, are both fully known before the row is built; starting from an entirely blank row and placing a star directly at each of those two indices produces exactly the right row, with no need to reason about contiguous runs at all. When the two indices coincide, in the middle row when n is odd, placing a star at the same position twice still leaves exactly one star there, so no special casing is needed for that overlap.

items: A blank row of n spaces is allocated once per row, replacing the need to build any contiguous run of stars at all.
A star is placed directly at index i, the main diagonal position, a single direct assignment rather than a column-by-column check.

A star is placed directly at index n minus 1 minus i, the anti diagonal position, using the exact same direct-placement technique, with the middle-row overlap handled naturally rather than through a special case.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n squared) total characters produced, the same as the brute force, since a blank row of length n is still needed, but with only two direct placements per row instead of n conditional checks.
Space: O(n), for the single row being built and printed at a time.
10. Further Optimization: A Single Output Call

Every row is already being built directly, so instead of printing each one separately, all n rows can be built first, joined together with newline characters, and the entire pattern can be produced with a single output call.

blocks.caption: Further optimization: join every row into one string and output it in a single call

items: Every row is still built by placing stars at its own two known columns, exactly as in the optimized version, the only change is collecting each finished row instead of printing it immediately.
Joining all n rows with newline characters assembles the complete X shape as a single string, entirely in memory, before any output call happens.
A single print call at the very end outputs the whole cross, cutting the operation count down to exactly 1 regardless of how large n is.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n squared), the same total characters produced.
Space: O(n squared), to hold every row joined into one string before the single output call. This trades some memory for the fewest possible output calls, exactly one, no matter how large n is.

blocks.text: When only a small, fixed number of positions in a row can ever hold a star, here always exactly two, it is far more direct to place stars at those known positions than to test every column against a condition. This same idea, knowing exactly where the interesting positions fall, comes up constantly in problems involving diagonals, corners, or fixed offsets.

items: Getting the anti diagonal formula wrong, it should be i plus j equals n minus 1, not n.
Forgetting that the two diagonal positions coincide exactly in the middle row when n is odd, which should still only print a single star there.
Off by one errors when placing stars directly into a preallocated row, especially in languages using fixed size character arrays.

blocks.text: Explicitly stating the two diagonal formulas, row equals column and row plus column equals n minus 1, before writing any code is a strong signal, these two conditions reappear constantly across grid based problems well beyond pattern printing.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text:
If the interviewer says "how many positions in a row can actually be a star", think: name the exact count, here always two, before deciding how to build the row.
If the interviewer says "can you avoid checking every column", think: start blank, place stars directly at the already-known indices.
If the interviewer says "what happens when the two positions coincide", think: placing a star at the same index twice is harmless, no special case is needed.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text: All three versions produce the same O(n squared) total characters, since that is fixed by the shape itself. What changes is how that output is organized: a two part diagonal check for every cell in the brute force version, two direct placements into a blank row in the optimized version, and exactly one call for the entire pattern in the further optimized version.

items: Pattern: grid pattern printing where only a small, fixed number of positions per row, here always exactly two, ever hold a star, so those exact positions can be placed directly instead of testing every column.

Core Idea: row i always has stars at exactly column i and column n minus 1 minus i, both known before the row is built, so starting from a blank row and placing a star at each of those two indices directly is far more efficient than testing every column against a condition.
Time: O(n squared) checks for the brute force, O(n) output calls for the optimized version, O(1) for the further optimized version; total characters printed are always O(n squared).
Space: O(1) extra for the brute force, O(n) for the current row, O(n squared) for the fully joined pattern.
Most Important Observation: when a shape's stars are isolated known points rather than a contiguous run, switch from building runs to placing values directly at known indices.
Interview Difficulty: easy to produce the correct shape with two nested conditions; explicitly naming the fixed count of star positions per row is what shows real pattern recognition.
One line memory trick: start blank, place a star at column i and column n minus 1 minus i.
